content: Ibalizumab is indicated for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in heavily treated adult patients who have multidrug-resistant infections and are failing their current antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimen. It is used in combination with other ART drugs. The recommended dosing includes a loading dose of 2,000 mg administered intravenously (IV) as a single dose, followed by a maintenance dose of 800 mg IV every two weeks, starting two weeks after the loading dose. The medication can be administered either as a diluted IV infusion or as an undiluted IV push. Dose modifications are not required when ibalizumab is used with other ART drugs or treatments. The safety and efficacy of ibalizumab have not been fully established. Common adverse effects include diarrhea (8%), dizziness (8%), nausea (5%), and rash (5%). Patients with a history of hypersensitivity reactions to ibalizumab or its components should not receive the drug. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) has been reported in one patient treated with ibalizumab in combination with other ARTs. During the initial phase of combination ART, patients with immune system recovery may develop an inflammatory response to latent or residual opportunistic infections, which may require further evaluation and treatment. Hypersensitivity reactions, including infusion-related and anaphylactic reactions, have been reported during post-approval use of ibalizumab. If signs or symptoms of anaphylaxis or other clinically significant hypersensitivity reactions occur, administration should be immediately discontinued, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. Although this registry does not specifically include ibalizumab, it likely includes data on concomitant antiretroviral drugs used by patients. Healthcare providers are encouraged to register patients by contacting the Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry (APR) at 1-800-258-4263. Based on animal studies, ibalizumab use during pregnancy may cause reversible immunosuppression in infants exposed in utero, including reductions in CD4+ T cell and B cell counts. Immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies, such as ibalizumab, are transported across the placenta in significant amounts, particularly near term, and may be transferred from the mother to the developing fetus. There are no available data on ibalizumab use in pregnant women to assess the risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Since IgG antibodies are increasingly transported across the placenta as pregnancy progresses, with the largest transfer occurring during the third trimester, administration of ibalizumab during pregnancy may affect immune responses in infants exposed in utero. Expert consultation is advised to guide monitoring and management, such as the need for antibiotic or immunoprophylaxis, based on the degree of immunosuppression observed. The safety of administering live or live-attenuated vaccines to exposed infants is unknown. It is not known whether ibalizumab is excreted into breast milk. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that HIV-1-infected mothers in the United States avoid breastfeeding to prevent postnatal transmission of HIV-1. Due to the potential for HIV transmission (in HIV-negative infants), the development of viral resistance (in HIV-positive infants), and adverse reactions in breastfed infants, mothers should be instructed not to breastfeed. Ibalizumab should be administered by a trained medical professional as an IV infusion or IV push. The preferred site for administration is the cephalic vein in the right or left arm. If this vein is not accessible, an appropriate vein located elsewhere may be used. For preparation, 33 mL of the drug is required to prepare the loading dose (2,000 mg) or maintenance doses (800 mg). The above information is provided for general informational and educational purposes only. For the most current formulary information, contact the applicable plan provider.
